intro: Pula's two remarkable trees both stand outside the city. On Veli Brijun, in Brijuni National Park, an olive split by a 1970s storm still gives oil every October; the park puts it at about 1,600 years from a 1960s carbon test, while others say only more than a thousand. It is a day trip by road to Fažana and the park's boat. In Medulin, south of Pula, a hackberry of about 115 years shades the main square and was Croatia's Tree of the Year in 2020.
meta_description: Old trees near Pula: the Brijuni olive, about 1,600 years by the park's figure, and Medulin's hackberry, Croatia's Tree of the Year 2020.
question_meta: The oldest tree near Pula is the olive on Veli Brijun, about 1,600 years by Brijuni National Park's figure, a dating others question.
question_answer: The oldest tree near Pula is the old olive on Veli Brijun in Brijuni National Park, which the park puts at about 1,600 years from a carbon-14 test made in the 1960s. Other sources say only that Brijuni's oldest olives are more than a thousand years old, and a new dating was announced in 2017.
question_context: Neither tree stands in Pula itself. The Brijuni olive is on Veli Brijun, the main island of Brijuni National Park, reached by road to Fažana, north-west of Pula, and then by the park's ticketed boat. The park says a trunk sample tested at the Ruđer Bošković Institute in Zagreb in the 1960s gave about 1,600 years. In 2017 the park, the Zagreb Faculty of Agriculture and the same institute announced a fresh dating of the islands' oldest olives, because the most anyone could say for certain was more than a thousand years; we have not found the results. The tree is about six metres tall, was split in two by a storm in the 1970s, and still yields about 30 kilograms of olives each October. The second tree is a Mediterranean hackberry on the main square of Medulin, at the southern tip of Istria, about 115 years old by local sources of 2020 and 2021. It won Croatia's Tree of the Year in 2020 and represented the country in the European contest in 2021. The two trees are a separate trip each.

faq.q: Can you visit the old olive on Brijuni?
faq.a: Yes, with a park ticket. Veli Brijun is reached only by the Brijuni National Park boat from Fažana, and the olive is on the visitor route. We have not confirmed current prices or crossing times.

faq.q: How old is the Brijuni olive?
faq.a: About 1,600 years by the park's figure, from a carbon-14 test made in the 1960s. Other sources say only more than a thousand years, and a new dating was announced in 2017.

faq.q: What is the tree on Medulin's main square?
faq.a: A Mediterranean hackberry of about 115 years, known as Najstarija Medulinka, the eldest resident of Medulin. It was Croatia's Tree of the Year in 2020.

trees.story:
A storm in the 1970s split this olive in two, and the park sealed the wounds with concrete. It still makes oil. Every October the old olive on Veli Brijun gives about 30 kilograms of fruit, which presses down to 4.1 kilograms of extra virgin oil, by Brijuni National Park's own count.

Its age is the park's figure, and it comes with a footnote. The park says a carbon-14 test on a sample of trunk wood, run at the Ruđer Bošković Institute in Zagreb in the 1960s, put it at about 1,600 years. Others are more careful. In 2017 the park, the Zagreb Faculty of Agriculture and the same institute announced they would date the islands' oldest olives afresh, because the most anyone could say for certain was more than a thousand years. We have not found the results. Somewhere between a thousand and sixteen hundred years is the honest answer.

It is not tall, about six metres, but its crown spreads some 22 metres one way and 8 the other. A genetics paper named it Brijunka and compared it with Istrian olive varieties, and the park describes it as a semi-wild form of the local Buža.

The only way here is the park's ticketed boat from Fažana, and the olive is on the visitor route. The newest photographs we have seen date from 2015, so if you have stood under it recently, tell us how it looks.
trees.access: Paid: Brijuni National Park, reached only by the park's ticketed boat; the olive is on the visitor route. Prices and hours not confirmed here.
trees.transport: Day trip from Pula: by road to Fažana, north-west of Pula, then the park boat to Veli Brijun (times not confirmed).
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk split in two, its old storm wounds filled with concrete, under a low crown about six metres high. It stands on Veli Brijun on the park's visitor route.
trees.verify_notes: AGE IS DISPUTED/SOFT. Park page says carbon analysis (C14) on a trunk wood sample gave about 1600 years; Rudjer Boskovic Institute Zagreb researched samples in the 1960s. The hrcak paper (SSR marker study, ~2010) calls it a 1600-year-old olive and compares it with Istrian cultivar Buga. Total Croatia News (2017-11-02) says Brijuni's olives are 'more than a thousand years old', the origin never properly researched, and that NP Brijuni, Zagreb Faculty of Agriculture and Rudjer Boskovic Institute planned to date the oldest trees (results not found). So write 'about 1,600 years by the park's figure (1960s radiocarbon), questioned', never a flat 1,600. Facts from the park page: height 6 m, crown projection 22 x 8 m (Croatia Post stamp text gives 26 m canopy, differs). Still fruits; October harvest averages 30 kg of olives giving 4.1 kg of extra virgin oil (park page). A storm in the 1970s split the trunk in two; the wounds were preserved with concrete. Park describes it as a semi-wild sub-variety of buza (Istrian autochthonous). Girth not stated by any fetched source. Alive: park page presents it as bearing fruit; the Commons photo is 2015, and the 2025 'Medic Tree Mapping' Commons category suggests a recent mapping. No recent dated source fetched, so flagged. Exact trunk coordinate relies on photo geotags.

trees.name: Najstarija Medulinka, the hackberry of Medulin
trees.story:
In 2020 more than 9,000 people voted for a village-square tree that is barely older than the First World War. The hackberry on Medulin's main square, known as Najstarija Medulinka, the eldest resident of Medulin, won Croatia's Tree of the Year with 9,373 of 23,238 votes. Second came a London plane in Mursko Središće, third an olive called Baka Maslina in Kaštel Štafilić.

In 2021 it represented Croatia in the European Tree of the Year under the title Chocolate Tree of our Memories, and finished tenth of fourteen. The prize for the national win was not a trophy but a check-up, an assessment of its health and structure by the Faculty of Forestry at the University of Zagreb.

Local sources put it at about 115 years in 2020 and 2021, which places its planting around 1905 or 1906. That is young for a species that, according to Total Croatia News, can live to around 400. What earns it a page is the life of the square around it. Medulin held its gatherings and celebrations in this shade, its young branches were once cut for walking sticks and tool handles, and its small fruits and leaves still turn up in folk medicine.

Nobody has published its height or girth, and the latest dated mention we found is from early 2021. If you sit under it, tell us how it is doing.

trees.access: Free, always open: it shades the public main square of Medulin.
trees.transport: Medulin is at the southern tip of Istria, south of Pula, by bus or car (times not confirmed); the tree is on the main square.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big hackberry shading Medulin's main square, the town's Tree of the Year in 2020.
trees.verify_notes: Young as these go (about 115 years in 2020/21, so planted around 1905 to 1906), earns its place as a community tree: Croatian Tree of the Year 2020 (9,373 of 23,238 votes, run by the Dubrovnik-Neretva protected-areas institution; second the London plane of Mursko Sredisce, third Baka Maslina of Kastel Stafilic), then Croatia's entry in European Tree of the Year 2021 (14 trees, rank 10, 31,283 votes per the contest page as logged in data/leads/_tree-of-the-year.json). Prize was a health and structure assessment by the Zagreb Faculty of Forestry. Gatherings and celebrations took place under it; TCN says the species can reach about 400 years. Planter, girth and height are not stated by any source seen. Age is as of 2020/21; add the years since. ALIVE: last dated sources are 2020 and early 2021; no 2024 or 2025 mention found, so flagged. Two sources (tourist board istra.hr and Total Croatia News) agree on species, age and place. Note the TotY page URL is truncated in our lead file.
